forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Up 1pp to 3%. Crisis deepened sharply on 12 May: ~70 Labour MPs publicly called for Starmer to resign or set a departure timetable; four ministerial aides quit; Foreign Sec Yvette Cooper and Home Sec Shabana Mahmood reportedly urged Starmer to oversee 'orderly transition' (Guardian). Cabinet meeting 12 May AM. CNBC/Eurasia Group analysts now say Starmer 'unlikely to last the year.' This is incrementally bullish for Labour-largest scenarios via a leadership-change reset (Cooper or Mahmood as new leader could re-anchor the centre-left vote and improve the late-2029 GE position) — but the central case remains a Reform-led Parliament. Confidence interval widens slightly upward to reflect the genuine possibility of a recovery story.
forecasts.base_rate: ~5-10% for a governing party 3+ years out polling third with this scale of local-election rout to recover to largest party
factors_up: Imminent leadership change (Cooper/Mahmood) could reset the Labour brand 3.5 years pre-election (+3pp)
Reform UK now has to govern dozens of councils — first failures could come quickly (+1pp)
First-past-the-post still rewards efficient vote distribution; Labour retains incumbent infrastructure (+1pp)
factors_down: Local elections showed historic 1,496-seat loss, 38 councils lost (-3pp)
YouGov has Labour third at 18%, behind Reform 25% and effectively tied with Con 17% (-2pp)
Open leadership crisis with cabinet revolt risks party split / disorganised handover (-2pp)
Reform-Conservative voter migration patterns make Labour pluralities harder under FPTP (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether Starmer is replaced in days, months, or hangs on through 2026
Identity and electoral profile of any successor (Cooper, Mahmood, Streeting)
Whether Reform-Con vote stays split or consolidates into a single right-wing bloc

update_triggers.up: Smooth Starmer transition to popular new leader; Labour polls return to 25%+; Reform fragments or hits governance scandal
update_triggers.down: Disorderly Labour split; Reform-Con pact forms; Labour polling falls into single digits

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 7%. Trump-Xi state visit confirmed for 13–15 May (talks 14–15) — i.e., starting tomorrow. Trump confirmed Taiwan arms sales will be on the agenda; Beijing has reportedly pressed for security commitments to be scaled back. Multiple analyses (CFR, CAP, Washington Times) frame the modal outcome as dialogue/horse-trading rather than escalation, even if the strategic picture remains dangerous. CFR notes China holds the upper hand at the summit, which paradoxically reduces near-term blockade probability (Beijing prefers to extract concessions diplomatically when leverage is high). Trump admin has not delivered the December $11B arms package, suggesting de-escalatory posture. Slight downgrade.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 39%. Underlying OBR March 2026 EFO unchanged: GDP growth 1.1% (2026), 1.6% (2027); GDP per person 1.1% to 2030; productivity unchanged from November (TFP unchanged, slight uplift from investment). The fresh datapoint is the Starmer leadership crisis on 12 May (~70 MPs in revolt, four aides resigned, cabinet challenge). Whoever leads Labour into 2029, the political turbulence — and possibility of a Reform or Reform-Con government — elevates fiscal/policy uncertainty for the 2030s decade. Asymmetric: more downside than upside (a Reform government is more likely to constrain net migration, which mechanically reduces GDP growth via labour supply). Slight downgrade.
